title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
claim: Early layers let projection onto top eigen-directions separate memorized from general performance, while late layers merge them inseparably.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared axes, contrasting first versus last layer
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same axes: accuracy from 0 to 1 against subspace dimension k from 0 to 200. Each shows three curves with open circle markers and shaded error bands: blue for train, green for test, and a dashed red for Gaussian (memorized) samples. Colored text labels sit next to the curves instead of a legend. Panel A, titled 'First layer', shows train and test rising quickly toward about 1.0 and 0.83. The red Gaussian curve stays near 0.1 until k is about 40, then climbs sigmoidally and joins train near k=120. Panel B, titled 'Last layer', shows all three curves jumping sharply at k of about 25. The red curve overlaps the blue one, and green plateaus lower. The eye goes first to the red curve lagging behind in panel A.
caption: Layer-dependent decoupling of memorization and generalization via Fisher projection: memorized Gaussian images. Classification accuracy as a function of the number of retained top Fisher eigenvectors $k$, computed over the full training set (CIFAR-10 and Gaussian images) for a single layer of a ResNet-20. Green: CIFAR-10 test; blue: CIFAR-10 train; red: memorized Gaussian samples. A) In the first layer, CIFAR-10 train and test accuracy rise in tandem and reach a maximum at $k\approx 45$, while accuracy on memorized Gaussian samples remains at $\approx\!30%$, demonstrating selective de-memorization at negligible cost to generalization. B) In the last layer, all three curves rise sharply even for very small $k$, with no separation between them at any point, indicating that memorized and structured representations have merged and can no longer be separated.
abstract: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.
